actSpeakBrief: Describing a chart you cannot see is the fastest test of whether an overview is doing its job.
actSpeak1: Describe a chart to your partner without showing it and without one figure. They sketch what they think it looks like. Compare, then swap.
actSpeak2: Take thirty seconds and any chart from the news. Give the introduction and the overview aloud, nothing else. Your partner times you.
actSpeak3: One of you argues the overview belongs second, the other that it belongs last. Argue it on what each costs you in the exam room.
actWriteBrief: A chart shows monthly sales of four drink types at one café across last year. Write the introduction and the overview — then write both a second way, so you can compare them. No figures in either.
resStrong: Strong work — the rule has landed.
resMid: Solid start. Worth one more pass.
resLow: Review the language focus slides, then try again.
coverSub: The introduction and the overview — the two paragraphs that decide your Task Achievement band, written before you describe a single figure.
s1ColA: A Task 1 report has four paragraphs. The first two come before any detail: an introduction saying what the chart shows, and an overview saying what it mainly shows.
s1ColB: Write them first and the body has somewhere to go. Write them last and they turn into a summary of what you have already said — which is why so many reports repeat themselves.
s1Note: The overview is the one paragraph you cannot leave out. A report without one is capped on Task Achievement, however good the rest of it is.
s2ColA: Take the prompt and change the nouns and the verb, reordering if it helps. One sentence is enough. Two is the most this paragraph is worth.
s2ColB: Leave alone: the figures, the units, the dates and any proper nouns. Changing 1990 into 1991, or a percentage into a number, is not paraphrase — it is an error.
s2Note: Words lifted straight from the prompt are not counted toward your 150. Copy the whole first line and you can be twenty words short without knowing it.
s3Title: The overview names the big picture
s3ColA: Two or three sentences on what a reader would notice from across the room: the highest and the lowest, the overall direction, the widest gap, the point where something turns.
s3ColB: No specific figures. Figures are the body’s job. An overview full of numbers is a body paragraph that has wandered up to the top of the page.
s3Note: It may sit straight after the introduction or right at the end. Both are accepted. Straight after is safer — you cannot then run out of time and lose it.
s5Title: Which one is doing an overview’s work?
s6ColA: Highest and lowest. Which category leads and which trails, across the whole period.
s6ColB: Overall direction. Up, down, flat — or one of each, if they differ.
s6ColC: The widest gap. Where the distance between categories is greatest.
s6ColD: The turning point. Where a line changes direction, or two lines cross.
s6Note: Two of these are enough for an overview at 150 words. Use all four and it becomes a body paragraph in disguise.
s9Title: Say it in your own words
s9Ctx: The prompt says shows and between 1990 and 2010. Replace both without touching the data.
s10Ctx: Two words an examiner is actively looking for when they reach your second paragraph.
s11Title: Every chart type has its own big picture
s11Ctx: Click a chart type on the left, then what its overview should say.
s12Title: The same two moves in Task 2
s13Ctx: Introduction first, then overview. Click the parts in order.
branchLocked: Your ledger does not support this ending
x06a: Every content word has moved — shows to illustrates, percentage to rates, countries to nations — while the dates and the number three stay exactly as given.
x06b: Only which has changed. Thirteen of its fourteen words are lifted straight from the prompt, and lifted words are not counted toward your 150.
x06c: This paraphrases the wording but breaks the data: owned is not bought their first, several is not three, and before 2010 is not 1990 to 2010.
x06d: A general opinion about the topic. An introduction reports what the chart contains, not what the writer thinks about cars.
x07a: A single reading at a single date. True, precise, and body-paragraph work — an overview that starts here has started describing.
x07b: A five-year span and an exact figure. The overview stands back from detail like this; the body is where it earns marks.
x07c: A direction that holds for every category, plus the one category that stands out. That is the whole job, and it needs no figures to do it.
x07d: Announcing what you are about to do is not the same as saying it. This sentence could sit above any chart and tells the reader nothing.
x09a: Length is not the problem — one sentence is a perfectly good introduction. The problem is whose sentence it is.
x09b: It is the prompt, word for word — below gives it away, because the table sits below the question, not below your answer. Copied words are discounted from the count, so a report that looks like 155 words may be marked as 142.
x09c: Mentioning all four is correct here. It is the overview that selects; the introduction says what the chart contains.
x09d: The present tense is right for describing what a table shows, whatever year the data covers. Tense is not the fault here.
x10a: Returns are part of the chart, so the overview may certainly mention them. What it should not do is quote their values.
x10b: Overall is the standard opening word for an overview and examiners look for it. Keep it.
x10c: Covering both categories is right — an overview describes the whole chart. Two trends in one sentence is good practice.
x10d: Four figures in one sentence. The overview should say sales rose and returns fell — the numbers are what the body is for.
x11a: Illustrates is the commonest safe swap for shows; depicts, presents and compares all work. Repeating shows throws away the easiest paraphrase on the page.
x11b: Covers or spans turns between 1990 and 2010 into your own words while leaving the dates themselves untouched — which is exactly the line to walk.
x12a: Overall is the conventional signal that the overview has begun. In general and broadly do the same work. Starting without one leaves the examiner hunting for the paragraph.
x12b: Striking or noticeable — naming the biggest feature as the biggest feature is the overview’s whole job. Do not make the reader work it out.
x13a: The four moves are the same everywhere; which one fits depends on what the chart is shaped like. A line graph is about direction, a single bar chart cannot be — it has no time to move through.
x14a: Naming the two sides is useful in a discussion essay, but it is not yet a position, and an essay that never takes one loses on Task Response.
x14b: The thesis. Task 2’s second move is the same shape as Task 1’s overview — say the big thing before you argue it, then hold to it.
x14c: A reason belongs in the body, where it can be developed. Spending it in the introduction leaves the first body paragraph with nothing new.
x14d: A rhetorical question postpones the position rather than stating it. The examiner is looking for a claim, not a second question.
x15a: Introduction first — what the chart shows, in your own words, dates intact. Then Overall, the direction that holds for every factory, and the one factory that stands out. Six pieces, two paragraphs, no figures at all.
x16a: Last is allowed, but making it the only option is wrong — and it is the riskier of the two, because it is the paragraph you lose if you run out of time.
x16b: Joined to the introduction it stops being a paragraph an examiner can point at. Keep the two moves visibly separate on the page.
x16c: Both positions are accepted. Second is safer: an overview you have already written cannot be lost to the clock, and the body then has a claim to support.
x16d: The word alone does not make a paragraph an overview, and position is not free — a summary buried mid-body will not be read as one.
